weak-acids-bases-s1.title: Ka values of four acids
weak-acids-bases-s1.text: Acid dissociation constants at 25 °C. Each acid gives up one proton: HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻.

weak-acids-bases-s2.title: Three acid solutions of equal volume
weak-acids-bases-s2.html: Key: HA a whole acid molecule; H₃O⁺ hydronium; A⁻ the anion left when HA loses a proton. Water is not drawn. Each box holds one kind of acid.

weak-acids-bases-s3.title: A household ammonia solution
weak-acids-bases-s3.text:
A cleaning solution is 0.15 M aqueous ammonia, NH₃, at 25 °C. For NH₃, Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵.

NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

items.q: What is the pH of 0.20 M acetic acid?

mistakes.why: Value: you treated acetic acid as strong. Only a small fraction ionizes; set up Ka = x² / (0.20 − x).
Value: you forgot the square root. Ka = x²/C, so x = √(Ka × C).

why.correct: Ka = x² / (0.20 − x) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Assume x ≪ 0.20: x = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.20) = 1.90 × 10⁻³ M = [H₃O⁺]. Check: 0.9% of 0.20, under 5%, so the assumption holds. pH = −log(1.9 × 10⁻³) = 2.72.

items.q: For 0.10 M solutions of each acid, which has the highest pH?
options: Hypochlorous acid
Hydrofluoric acid
Nitrous acid
Acetic acid

why.correct: At equal concentration, the acid with the smallest Ka ionizes least, makes the least H₃O⁺ and so has the highest pH. HOCl has Ka = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸.
options: Right: the smallest Ka, the least H₃O⁺.
HF has the largest Ka here, so it gives the most H₃O⁺ and the lowest pH.
HNO₂ has the second-largest Ka, so its pH is low.
Acetic acid ionizes more than HOCl (Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ vs 3.0 × 10⁻⁸), so its pH is lower.

items.q: What is the percent ionization of 0.050 M HNO₂? (Check whether the small-x assumption is valid.)

mistakes.why: Value: the small-x shortcut is off by more than 5% here. Solve the quadratic x² + Ka·x − Ka·C = 0.

why.correct: Small x gives x = √(4.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.050) = 4.47 × 10⁻³ M, which is 8.9% of 0.050: over 5%, so solve x² + (4.0 × 10⁻⁴)x − 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 0. x = 4.28 × 10⁻³ M. Percent ionization = x / 0.050 × 100 = 8.6%.

items.q: What is Kb for the fluoride ion, F⁻? Give your answer in scientific notation.

mistakes.why: Value: Kb is not 1/Ka. For a conjugate pair Ka × Kb = Kw, so Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / Ka.
Value: you divided Ka by Kw. Rearrange Ka × Kb = Kw to Kb = Kw / Ka.

why.correct: F⁻ is the conjugate base of HF. Ka × Kb = Kw, so Kb = (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) / (6.8 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.5 × 10⁻¹¹.

items.q: Which of the four conjugate bases, OCl⁻, CH₃COO⁻, NO₂⁻ and F⁻, is the strongest base?
options: OCl⁻
F⁻
NO₂⁻
CH₃COO⁻

why.correct: Kb = Kw / Ka, so the weakest acid has the strongest conjugate base. HOCl has the smallest Ka, so OCl⁻ has the largest Kb (about 3.3 × 10⁻⁷).
options: Right: smallest Ka, largest Kb.
This assumes a strong acid has a strong conjugate base. It is the reverse: HF has the largest Ka, so F⁻ has the smallest Kb.
HNO₂ has a large Ka, so NO₂⁻ is a weak base.
Acetate is a stronger base than F⁻ or NO₂⁻, but HOCl is a weaker acid than acetic acid, so OCl⁻ is stronger still.

items.q: Which box represents a strong acid?
options: Box 2
Box 1
Box 3
Box 3, which has the fewest acid molecules

why.correct: A strong acid ionizes fully, so no HA molecules remain. Only Box 2 has none.
options: Right: only ions, no whole molecules.
Box 1 is mostly whole HA molecules: a weak acid.
Box 3 still has whole HA molecules: a weak acid.
Fewer acid molecules means a more dilute solution, not a stronger acid; Box 3 still holds whole HA molecules.

items.q: Boxes 1 and 3 contain the same acid at the same temperature. Which statement is best supported?
options: Box 3 is the more dilute solution, and a larger fraction of its acid is ionized
Box 3 has the larger Ka, because a larger fraction of its acid is ionized
Box 1 has the lower pH, because it contains more acid molecules
Both boxes have the same percent ionization, because they hold the same acid

why.correct: Box 1: 1 of 7 acid particles ionized (14%); Box 3: 1 of 4 (25%), with fewer acid particles in the same volume, so it is more dilute. Diluting a weak acid raises its percent ionization: Q = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] falls below Ka on dilution, so more HA ionizes.
options: Right: fewer particles per volume, a larger fraction ionized.
Ka is fixed for an acid at a given temperature; it does not change with concentration.
Both have one H₃O⁺ in the same volume, so the same pH. Whole HA molecules do not lower the pH.
Percent ionization depends on concentration as well as on the acid.

items.q: Treat Box 1 as an equilibrium mixture in which each particle drawn stands for 0.010 mol in 1.0 L. What is Ka for this acid?

options: Right: equilibrium concentrations of both products over the reactant.
This leaves out one product: Ka has [H₃O⁺] and [A⁻] in the numerator.
This uses the starting amount of HA (7 particles), not the 6 left at equilibrium.
This leaves out the denominator [HA].

items.q: Which statements about Box 1 are true? Select all that apply.
options: [HA] is greater than [A⁻]
[H₃O⁺] equals the starting concentration of the acid
The acid is mostly un-ionized
Adding water would lower its percent ionization

why.correct: Six whole molecules against one ionized: [HA] > [A⁻], and the acid is mostly un-ionized, which is what makes it weak.
options: Right: 6 HA to 1 A⁻.
That is true of a strong acid. Here [H₃O⁺] is only 1/7 of the acid added.
Right: the defining feature of a weak acid.
Dilution raises the percent ionization of a weak acid.

items.q: What is [OH⁻] in the solution? Include the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: ammonia is a weak base; only a small fraction reacts. Use Kb = x² / (0.15 − x).
Value: take the square root: x² = Kb × C.

why.correct: Kb = x² / (0.15 − x) ≈ x² / 0.15, so x = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.15) = 1.64 × 10⁻³ M = [OH⁻] (1.1% of 0.15, so the approximation holds). Rounded: 1.6 × 10⁻³ M.

items.q: What is the pH of the ammonia cleaning solution?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pOH. The solution is basic: pH = 14.00 − pOH.
Value: you treated NH₃ as a strong base. Only about 1% of it reacts with water.

items.q: What is the pKa of NH₄⁺, the conjugate acid of ammonia?

mistakes.why: Value: that is pKb of NH₃. For the conjugate acid, pKa = 14.00 − pKb.

why.correct: pKb = −log(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.745. pKa + pKb = pKw = 14.00, so pKa = 14.00 − 4.74 = 9.26. (Equivalently Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰.)

items.q: A student says, "Ammonia is a weak base, so its solution must be close to neutral." Which response is best?
options: "Weak" means only a small fraction reacts, but 0.15 M NH₃ still makes enough OH⁻ to give pH 11.2
"Weak" means the solution is dilute, so the pH is close to 7
Weak bases make H₃O⁺ instead of OH⁻, so the pH is below 7
Weak bases react fully with water, so the pH is very high

why.correct: Weak describes the fraction that reacts (about 1% here), not the pH. Even 1% of 0.15 M is 1.6 × 10⁻³ M OH⁻, far above water's 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M.
options: Right: weak is about extent of reaction, not about being near neutral.
Weak and dilute are different ideas: a 15 M ammonia solution is concentrated and still weak.
NH₃ accepts a proton from water, which leaves OH⁻; the solution is basic.
Reacting fully would make it a strong base.

items.q: A 0.085 M solution of a weak acid HA has pH 3.25. What is Ka? Give your answer in scientific notation.

mistakes.why: Value: square [H₃O⁺]. Both H₃O⁺ and A⁻ are in the numerator, and they are equal: Ka = x² / (C − x).

items.q: Put the steps for finding the pH of a weak acid solution from Ka and its concentration in order.
options: Write the ionization equation and the Ka expression
Set up an ICE table: change −x for HA, +x for H₃O⁺ and A⁻
Assume x is small and solve x = √(Ka × C)
Check that x is under 5% of C (otherwise solve the quadratic)
pH = −log x

why.correct: Equation and expression, ICE table, small-x estimate, the 5% check, then the log. The check comes before you trust x.

items.q: Solution 1 is 0.10 M HCl and Solution 2 is 0.10 M HF. Each is diluted tenfold. How do their pH values change?
options: HCl rises by 1.0 unit; HF rises by less than 1.0 unit
Both rise by exactly 1.0 unit
HCl rises by 1.0 unit; HF rises by more than 1.0 unit
Neither changes, because Ka and Kw do not change

why.correct: HCl ionizes fully, so [H₃O⁺] falls tenfold and pH rises by 1.0. For HF, dilution makes Q < Ka, so more HF ionizes and partly offsets the dilution: [H₃O⁺] falls only by about √10, and pH rises by about 0.5.
options: Right: dilution raises the percent ionization of the weak acid.
Only the strong acid follows the one-unit rule; the weak acid ionizes more when diluted.
The extra ionization of HF on dilution makes its pH rise less, not more.
K values stay the same, but concentrations change, so pH changes.

items.q: Which claim correctly explains why acetic acid is classified as a weak acid?
options: Ka is much less than 1, so at equilibrium most acetic acid molecules are un-ionized
Its solutions have a pH above 7
Each acetic acid molecule has one ionizable hydrogen
Its solutions are usually dilute

why.correct: Weak means the ionization equilibrium lies to the left (Ka ≪ 1): most molecules stay as HA. Stating "Ka < 1, mostly un-ionized" is what readers look for, not just "weak Ka".
options: Right: small Ka, mostly un-ionized.
Any acid solution has a pH below 7.
HCl also has one ionizable hydrogen and is strong; the count does not decide strength.
Weak and dilute are different: concentration does not change Ka.

items.q: What is the pH of 0.25 M NaOCl? (Ka of HOCl = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸.)

mistakes.why: Value: OCl⁻ is a base, not an acid. Find Kb = Kw/Ka and solve for [OH⁻].
Value: that is the pOH. Subtract it from 14.00.
